When Ms. Okafor posted the debate assignments on the classroom door, Priya read her name twice to make sure there was no mistake. The question for the sixth-grade tournament was whether the town should convert the empty lot on Birch Avenue into a parking garage. Priya had spent the entire fall collecting signatures to transform that lot into a neighborhood park, yet she had been assigned to argue in favor of the garage.

"This has to be an error," she protested after class. "Everyone knows my opinion."

"That is exactly why it is the right assignment," her teacher replied. "Anyone can defend a position she already holds, but a real debater understands the opposing side well enough to argue it."

For the first few days, Priya worked grudgingly. She typed a few weak arguments and spent the rest of her research time reading about parks. Eventually her partner, Desmond, lost patience with her. "If we walk in there with this, we will lose in five minutes," he warned, tapping the single page. "Do you want to lose, or do you want to learn something?"

That night Priya forced herself to call her uncle, who owned a bakery two blocks from the lot, expecting him to agree with her. Instead, he described customers who circled the block for twenty minutes and then drove away in frustration. He also told her about the pharmacy that had closed the previous spring because older shoppers could not find anywhere to park. By the time she hung up, her notebook was full, and her stomach felt uneasy.

At the tournament, Priya spoke clearly and calmly about the empty storefronts and the discouraged shoppers. She answered every question from the opposing team, even the difficult ones about trees and playgrounds, because she had already asked herself those same questions. When the judges announced that she and Desmond had won, she felt proud, but not exactly happy.

On the bus ride home, Desmond asked whether she had changed her mind about the park.

Priya gazed out the window at the passing shops. "No," she said slowly. "I still believe the town needs green space, but I no longer think the people who want the garage are foolish."

The following week, she presented a new petition at the town meeting. It requested a small park with a row of parking spaces along one side.
stem: Which statement best expresses a theme of the story?
choices: Winning a competition is the best way to prove that your opinion is correct.
Understanding an opposing view can make your own beliefs wiser.
People should never change their opinions once they have taken a public stand.
Adults usually understand town problems better than young people do.
explanation: Priya keeps her goal of a park, but studying the garage side teaches her to respect it and leads to a compromise. The other statements are not developed by the story.

Nadia had planned her science fair project down to the last detail. She would grow bean plants under three colors of light, red, blue, and green, and demonstrate that blue light produced the tallest, healthiest plants. Three articles had predicted exactly that result, so all she needed was the evidence.

For four weeks she measured her plants every afternoon and recorded each height in a spiral notebook. Then, during the third week, the plants under the blue bulb began to droop, and their leaves turned pale yellow and curled at the edges. By the end of the month, the tallest plants on the shelf were the ones under red light, while the blue plants looked as if they had given up.

Nadia stared at her notebook in dismay. The fair was only four days away, and her results were the complete opposite of her prediction.

"Just leave out the blue plants," suggested her brother, Karim. "Say something broke and show the other two."

"That would be dishonest," Nadia answered, although she did not sound entirely certain.

That evening she sat beside the shelf with a flashlight, examining every part of her setup for a clue. The soil was moist, and the timers on the lamps were working properly. Then she held her hand beneath the blue lamp and immediately pulled it away. She had purchased that bulb at a different store, and it was an older type that produced a tremendous amount of heat. Her plants had not suffered because of the color of the light; they had been cooked.

Since there was no time to repeat the experiment, Nadia decided to do something that felt risky. She rewrote her poster, and across the top, in large letters, she printed "What Went Wrong, and What I Learned." Underneath, she explained her hypothesis, displayed every measurement, described the overheated bulb, and listed how she would control the temperature in a future experiment.

At the fair, one judge studied the poster silently for a long time while Nadia's palms grew damp. At last the judge looked up. "Do you know how many professional scientists make a mistake like this?" she asked. "Most of them, and the good ones write it down."

Nadia did not win first place, but she received an honorable mention. The judge's card, which she pinned above her desk, said simply, "Honest work."
stem: Which statement best expresses a theme of the story?
choices: Honesty about mistakes is part of doing good science.
Following a careful plan always guarantees the expected result.
Brothers and sisters should help each other with schoolwork.
First place is the only reward that matters at a science fair.
explanation: Nadia reports her failed results honestly and is praised for it by the judge. The story shows that careful plans can still go wrong, and Karim's advice is rejected.

By the spring of 1935, dust had been blowing across the Oklahoma plains for four long years, and twelve-year-old Ruth Dawson could hardly remember the color of growing wheat. Every morning she swept a gray film off the kitchen table, and by evening it had always returned. Her mother hung damp sheets over the windows and stuffed rags beneath the doors, but the powdery dust still crept inside, settling in the flour bin and in the folds of the blankets.

On a Sunday afternoon in April, the northern sky turned black. It was not an ordinary rain cloud but an enormous wall of dirt, hundreds of feet high, rolling toward the farm faster than a train. While the wind howled for hours, the family huddled in the dark kitchen with wet cloths pressed over their faces. When the storm finally ended, drifts of soil were piled against the barn like brown snow.

That night Ruth overheard her parents talking quietly at the table. Her uncle had written from California, where he was picking fruit, to report that there was steady work and the sky was always blue.

"We could leave next month," her mother said.

Ruth held her breath. Part of her wanted to go, because she was tired of grit between her teeth and of watching her father's shoulders sag as he walked through the ruined fields.

However, her father shook his head. "A man from the county office visited last week," he explained. "He says the soil blew away because farmers plowed up the prairie grass that used to hold it in place. The government will pay us to plow in curves along the hills and to plant rows of trees that slow the wind. If enough families cooperate, the land might recover."

"Might," her mother repeated.

"Might," he agreed.

They stayed. That autumn, Ruth and her father planted a line of thin cedar and elm seedlings along the edge of the north field. They hauled water from the well in heavy buckets, yet many of the young trees withered anyway, and Ruth decided the work was hopeless.

The following spring, however, she noticed tiny new leaves on the trees that had survived. Ruth knelt beside the nearest one and touched a leaf gently, as if it might blow away. For the first time in years, she allowed herself to imagine the field full of wheat.
stem: Which statement best summarizes the story?
choices: A farm family decides to move to California, where an uncle has found steady work picking fruit.
A girl learns that the dust storms on the plains are much less dangerous than most people believe.
A farm family survives years of dust storms and, through patient work, begins to hope again.
A farmer discovers that wheat grows best when it is planted in curved rows along the hills.
explanation: The family stays, plants trees, and at the end Ruth sees new leaves and imagines wheat again. They do not move, and the other choices are not supported.

Every morning she swept a gray film off the kitchen table, and by evening it had always returned. Her mother hung damp sheets over the windows and stuffed rags beneath the doors, but the powdery dust still crept inside, settling in the flour bin and in the folds of the blankets.

On a Sunday afternoon in April, the northern sky turned black. It was not an ordinary rain cloud but an enormous wall of dirt, hundreds of feet high, rolling toward the farm faster than a train. While the wind howled for hours, the family huddled in the dark kitchen with wet cloths pressed over their faces. When the storm finally ended, drifts of soil were piled against the barn like brown snow.

That night Ruth overheard her parents talking quietly at the table. Her uncle had written from California, where he was picking fruit, to report that there was steady work and the sky was always blue.

"We could leave next month," her mother said.

Ruth held her breath. Part of her wanted to go, because she was tired of grit between her teeth and of watching her father's shoulders sag as he walked through the ruined fields.

However, her father shook his head. "A man from the county office visited last week," he explained. "He says the soil blew away because farmers plowed up the prairie grass that used to hold it in place. The government will pay us to plow in curves along the hills and to plant rows of trees that slow the wind. If enough families cooperate, the land might recover."

"Might," her mother repeated.

"Might," he agreed.

A honeybee colony can contain more than forty thousand bees, but only some of them are foragers, the workers that fly out to collect nectar and pollen. When a forager finds a rich patch of flowers, the whole colony benefits if others can find it too. But how can a tiny insect tell her sisters where to fly? The answer is one of the most remarkable discoveries about animal behavior: bees dance.

In the 1940s, an Austrian scientist named Karl von Frisch spent years watching bees inside glass-walled hives. He noticed that a forager returning with food would often move in a strange pattern on the honeycomb. She would walk forward in a straight line while shaking her body from side to side, then circle back and repeat the movement. Von Frisch called this the "waggle dance."

Through careful experiments, he found that the dance contains a kind of code. The direction of the straight "waggle run" tells other bees which way to fly. The comb inside the hive hangs in a vertical position, and it is too dark to see the sky. So the dancer uses "straight up" on the comb to stand for the direction of the sun. If she waggles straight up, the flowers are toward the sun. If she waggles at an angle to the right of straight up, the flowers lie at that same angle to the right of the sun.

The length of the waggle run tells how far away the food is. A short run means the flowers are close, while a longer run signals a longer trip. Other bees crowd around the dancer and follow her movements with their antennae. They also smell the scent of the flowers on her body. Then they leave the hive and head for the spot she has described.

At first, many scientists doubted that an insect could share such detailed information. Later, researchers tested the idea by attaching tiny tags to bees and following their flights with radar. The tracks showed that bees that had watched a dance really did fly in the direction it described.

Von Frisch shared a Nobel Prize for his work in 1973. His discovery also matters today. Farmers depend on honeybees to pollinate crops such as apples and almonds. By understanding how bees find food, scientists can protect these insects and the harvests that rely on them.

For more than a thousand years, a network of trade routes connected China with the lands around the Mediterranean Sea. Today we call this network the Silk Road, even though it was not a single road and it carried much more than silk.

The name comes from China's most famous export. For centuries, the Chinese kept the method of making silk a closely guarded secret. Wealthy people as far away as Rome prized the smooth, shimmering cloth and paid enormous prices for it. In return, goods such as glass, silver, wool, and horses traveled east toward China.

Very few traders ever traveled the entire route, which stretched about four thousand miles. Instead, goods moved from one merchant to the next, a little like a baton in a relay race. A bolt of silk might change hands a dozen times before it reached a market in the west. Each merchant added to the price to earn a profit, so by the end of the journey the cloth cost far more than it had at the start.

The journey was difficult and often dangerous. Caravans crossed burning deserts, such as the Taklamakan, and climbed through freezing mountain passes. Traders depended on camels, which could carry heavy loads and go for days without water. Along the main routes, travelers stopped at inns called caravanserais. These walled inns were spaced about a day's journey apart, and they offered food, water, and a safe place to sleep.

Perhaps the most important cargo on the Silk Road could not be packed into a saddlebag. Ideas, beliefs, and inventions traveled with the merchants. Buddhism spread from India into China along these routes. The knowledge of how to make paper slowly moved west from China and eventually reached Europe. Foods such as grapes, peaches, and spices found new homes far from where they were first grown. Sadly, not everything that spread was welcome. Diseases also moved along the trade routes, sometimes with deadly results.

In time, ships began to carry more goods by sea, and the overland routes became less important. Still, the Silk Road had shown that trade does more than move objects. When people exchange goods, they also exchange ideas, and those ideas can change the world.

In 1912, a German scientist named Alfred Wegener proposed an idea that most experts thought was ridiculous. He claimed that all of the continents had once been joined together in one giant landmass, which he later called Pangaea. Over millions of years, he said, the pieces had slowly drifted apart.

Wegener did not invent this idea out of thin air. He had collected several kinds of evidence. First, he pointed out that the coastlines of South America and Africa fit together like pieces of a puzzle. Second, fossils of the same plants and animals had been found on continents now separated by wide oceans. One example was Mesosaurus, a small reptile that lived in fresh water. Its fossils appear in both Brazil and southern Africa, yet it could never have swum across a salty ocean. Third, he found signs that glaciers had once covered parts of Africa and India, places that are hot today.

Even so, most scientists rejected his idea. The main problem was that Wegener could not explain what force was strong enough to push entire continents. He suggested that the continents plowed through the rocky ocean floor like ships through ice, but other experts showed that this was impossible. Without a believable cause, they refused to accept his theory. Wegener kept gathering evidence until he died on a research trip to Greenland in 1930.

The answer came from the bottom of the sea. In the 1950s and 1960s, scientists used sound waves to map the ocean floor. They discovered long underwater mountain ranges where hot rock rises from deep inside Earth. As this rock cools, it forms new ocean floor, which slowly spreads away from the ridge on both sides.

These discoveries led to the theory of plate tectonics. According to this theory, Earth's outer layer is broken into huge plates that move a few inches each year. The continents ride along on top of these plates. The theory also explained why most earthquakes and volcanoes happen near the edges of the plates.

Today, Wegener is remembered as a scientist who was right about the big idea, even though he was wrong about how it worked. His story shows that science can change its mind when new evidence appears.
